content.title: Maundy Thursday History, Facts & the Holy Week | Study.com
content.text: Explore the history of Holy Thursday. Find out what Maundy Thursday is and understand its role during Holy Week. Discover interesting facts about Holy Thursday. FAQ What happens on Holy Thursday? On Holy Thursday, the diocese bishop celebrates a daytime Mass to bless all the holy oils used during the church year. After sundown, the Mass of the Lord's Supper begins, a special celebration remembering the day Christ instituted the Holy Eucharist and the priesthood. What is Maundy Thursday, and why do we celebrate it? Maundy Thursday or Holy Thursday is the day commemorating Christ's Last Supper with His apostles before His crucifixion. It is the second most sacred Mass celebration of the year after Easter. Why is Holy Thursday called Maundy Thursday? The word "maundy" comes from the Latin translation of the Bible verse, "I give you a new commandment," or Maundatum novum da vobis. This was among Jesus' last words to His followers in the Gospel of John. Maundy Thursday, also known as Holy Thursday or Sheer Thursday, celebrates the Last Supper of Jesus Christ the day before His crucifixion. It occurs on the Thursday of Holy Week and is also the beginning of the Easter Triduum. Most prominently in the Catholic and Orthodox Churches, the celebration commemorates the institution of the Eucharist, or Jesus giving His Body and Blood under the appearance of bread and wine at every Mass. In conjunction with this, Holy Thursday remembers Christ's establishment of the priesthood, whereby His apostles were given authority to perform this miracle and pass it on to other men in the ordination of priests and bishops. The word "maundy" comes from the Latin maundatum, in the phrase, Maundatum novum da vobis, or "I give you a new commandment," the words Jesus speaks to His apostles in the Gospel of John. Converts to Christianity in the ancient Roman world recognized the significance of the Last Supper of Christ through the apostles' teaching. They celebrated the day with prayer, reception of Holy Communion at Mass, and blessing of holy oils or chrism that would be used to baptize and confirm new church members at the Easter celebration and throughout the year. Today bishops perform the same blessing of the oils on Holy Thursday morning, with the Mass of the Lord's Supper taking place after sundown. During this time, the priest will ceremonially wash the feet of twelve men to remember Christ's washing of his apostles' feet at the Last Supper. To unlock this lesson you must be a Study.com member Create an account Maundy Thursday is part of Holy Week, also known as Passion Week, the concluding period of Lent, a time of fasting and abstinence in preparation for Easter. The Holy Week timeline begins on Palm Sunday when Jesus entered Jerusalem to celebrate the feast of Passover with His disciples. He rode on a donkey as crowds cheered Him as the coming Messiah who would save the Jews from their oppression. Later in the week, Holy Wednesday or Spy Wednesday commemorates the beginning of Judas' betrayal, an apostle of Jesus who led the temple guards to where Jesus was resting. Some facts about these and the influence of the Holy Thursday commemoration include the following: To unlock this lesson you must be a Study.com member Create an account Holy Week is the final week of Lent leading into the celebration of Easter and Christ's Resurrection. It includes Holy Thursday or Maundy Thursday, the fifth day of the week, and the celebration of the Last Supper of Christ with His apostles, marking the institution of the Eucharist and the priesthood. This Mass remains the most sacred in the church year after Easter and precedes the day celebrating Christ's passion and death on Good Friday. The word "maundy" comes from the Latin Maundatum novum da vobis or "I give you a new commandment" from John's Gospel. In its entirety, Holy Week also includes Palm Sunday, when Christ rode triumphantly into Jerusalem, Holy Wednesday, when Judas arranged for Jesus' betrayal; and the Easter Triduum, the three days that include Holy Thursday, Good Friday, and Holy Saturday, during which time Christ said farewell to his apostles and was arrested by the Jews before being turned over the Romans and crucified. The Triduum ends at sundown on Holy Saturday, when the celebration of the Easter Vigil begins. Traditions on Holy Thursday include washing the feet of twelve people at Mass to symbolize Jesus washing His own apostles' feet. Silent prayer or adoration usually follows the Mass, and the faithful prepare for Good Friday.
